n-m-h3-prob-02.title: Two events wey no fit happen together: dem independent?
n-m-h3-prob-02.goal: Tell apart "no fit happen together" from "independent," and explain using meaning of independence (knowing one no change probability of the other).
n-m-h3-prob-02.material: Dem roll fair die one time. Event A na "roll 1 or 2," and B na "roll 3 or 4." The two events no fit happen at same time. Jimin look this and make claim below.
n-m-h3-prob-02.thinking.0: Judge whether claim correct using evidence
n-m-h3-prob-02.s.s1.prompt: Jimin talk, "Events A and B no fit happen at same time, so dem no affect each other. So dem independent." Which assessment of Jimin claim most appropriate?
n-m-h3-prob-02.s.s1.hint.0: Think yourself wetin happen to chance of B once you know A happen.
n-m-h3-prob-02.s.s1.hint.1: If dem independent, knowing A must leave probability of B same as before. Compare whether this na the situation here.
n-m-h3-prob-02.s.s1.o.a: Wrong. If you know A happen, B no fit happen again, so probability of B don change from before.
n-m-h3-prob-02.s.s1.o.b: Correct. Since both events no happen together, one no change probability of the other.
n-m-h3-prob-02.s.s1.r.b: You read "no fit happen together" as "no affect each other." One event making the other impossible na strong effect itself.
n-m-h3-prob-02.s.s1.o.c: Correct. Since A and B get same probability, one no affect the other.
n-m-h3-prob-02.s.s1.r.c: Equal-size probabilities and independence na separate things. Independence ask whether probability of one event change when you know the other.
n-m-h3-prob-02.s.s1.o.d: Wrong. Since A and B get different probabilities, one affect the other.
n-m-h3-prob-02.s.s1.r.d: Different probabilities no mean events no independent. The thing to compare na whether chance of one change when you know the other.
n-m-h3-prob-02.s.s1.explain: If A and B no fit happen at same time, and both get probability bigger than 0, then knowing A happen change probability of B to 0. If dem independent, P(B|A)=P(B) must hold, so dem no independent. For die, A be 1 or 2 and B be 3 or 4; P(B)=1/3, but if A happen, P(B|A)=0.
n-m-h3-prob-02.s.s2.prompt: With same die roll, also consider event C (even number) and D (roll 3 or less). Choose all pairs of events wey dey independent from each other.
n-m-h3-prob-02.s.s2.hint.0: For each pair, find P(both happen) and P(first)×P(second), and compare whether dem equal.
n-m-h3-prob-02.s.s2.hint.1: First write rolls belonging to each event, then find rolls belonging to both events.
n-m-h3-prob-02.s.s2.r.a: You treat pair wey no fit happen together as independent. If one happen, probability of the other become 0.
n-m-h3-prob-02.s.s2.r.d: You treat A dey inside D as "unrelated." If A happen, D must happen, so probability of D change.
n-m-h3-prob-02.s.s2.explain: P(A)=1/3, P(C)=1/2, and P(A∩C)=P({2})=1/6=P(A)P(C), so A and C independent. B and C independent too, because B∩C={4} and 1/6=1/3×1/2. For A and D, P(A∩D)=1/3 but P(A)P(D)=1/6, so dem no independent. Events fit be independent even when dem overlap, and events wey no overlap (when probabilities bigger than 0) no fit be independent.
n-m-h3-prob-02.s.s3.prompt: Write explanation to send Jimin. Using what it mean for A and B to be independent, explain why A and B no independent in this die example, with phrase "chance of B when we know A happen."
n-m-h3-prob-02.s.s3.hint.0: First write which die rolls remain when you know A happen, and check whether any of dem belong to B.
n-m-h3-prob-02.s.s3.hint.1: Put original probability of B and probability after that side by side in one sentence, then compare dem.
n-m-h3-prob-02.s.s3.placeholder: e.g. If you know A happen, then B ...
n-m-h3-prob-02.s.s3.selfAssess.0: You write meaning of independence as "knowing one event no change chance of the other"?
n-m-h3-prob-02.s.s3.selfAssess.1: For this example, you state both original chance of B and its chance after learning A happen?
n-m-h3-prob-02.s.s3.selfAssess.2: You say "no fit happen at same time" and "independent" different things?
n-m-h3-prob-02.s.s3.model.0: If events independent, chance of B stay 1/3 even after we know A happen. But if A (1 or 2) happen, B (3 or 4) no fit happen, so its probability become 0. Probability change, so dem no independent.
n-m-h3-prob-02.s.s3.model.1: At first, chance of B na one-third. But if we learn die show 1 or 2, then 3 or 4 impossible, so chance of B change to 0. If dem independent e no suppose change, but e change, so dem no independent.

n-m-h3-prob-08.material: Team A and Team B dey play match where the first team to win 3 games take all the 80,000-won prize, but something interrupt dem. n-m-h3-prob-08.thinking.1: Set up an equal-chance sample space
n-m-h3-prob-08.thinking.2: Explain why assumption no dey change result
n-m-h3-prob-08.s.s1.prompt: Team A and Team B dey play match where the first team to win 3 games take all the 80,000-won prize, but interruption happen. So far Team A don win 2 games and Team B don win 1. Dem go share prize according to each team chance of winning. Choose all the information we need to find these probabilities. (We no know anything about the teams' skill.)
n-m-h3-prob-08.s.s1.hint.0: Remove each piece of information one by one and think whether we still fit calculate future winning chance without am.
n-m-h3-prob-08.s.s1.hint.1: Write wetin you need to know to find how many more games each team gats win to become champion.

n-m-h3-prob-08.s.s1.r.a: You think say the order matter. Future winning chance depend on current win counts and the games wey remain; the order wey dem gather wins no get effect.
n-m-h3-prob-08.s.s1.o.b: How many wins each team don get so far (2 wins and 1 win)
n-m-h3-prob-08.s.s1.o.c: How many wins dem need to become champion (first team to 3 wins)
n-m-h3-prob-08.s.s1.o.d: How long the match don take so far

n-m-h3-prob-08.s.s1.o.e: The chance say each team go win one game
n-m-h3-prob-08.s.s1.explain: The current win counts and wins needed to become champion show how many more games each team gats win (A need 1 game, B need 2 games), and per-game winning chance determine probability of that happening. Win order and time no dey affect remaining games, so dem no need.
n-m-h3-prob-08.s.s2.prompt: Suppose both teams get equal chance to win one game and games no dey affect one another. Find probability say Team A go win the championship, and write the prize money Team A suppose get. Include the cases wey you count in your answer.
n-m-h3-prob-08.s.s2.hint.0: Write wetin gats happen in the remaining games for Team A to win and for Team B to win.
n-m-h3-prob-08.s.s2.hint.1: Even if match fit end early, think whether imagining say dem play all the remaining games fit make the cases get equal chance.
n-m-h3-prob-08.s.s2.selfAssess.0: You consider the cases where Team A win and where Team B win separately?
n-m-h3-prob-08.s.s2.selfAssess.1: You choose cases wey each get the same chance?
n-m-h3-prob-08.s.s2.selfAssess.2: You split the prize money according to the probabilities?
n-m-h3-prob-08.s.s2.model.0: If we imagine dem play both remaining games, the four outcomes (A,A), (A,B), (B,A), (B,B) get the same chance. For B to win, B gats win both games, na only (B,B), so B get 1/4 and A get 3/4. So A suppose get 60,000 won and B 20,000 won.
n-m-h3-prob-08.s.s2.model.1: For B to win, B gats win the two remaining games one after another, and that chance na 1/2×1/2=1/4. So probability say A win na 3/4, and A suppose get 60,000 won from the 80,000-won prize.
n-m-h3-prob-08.s.s3.prompt: Minji talk, "If A win the next game, match go end, so e no right to imagine say dem play both remaining games, because na different from wetin go really happen." Which reply best fit her statement?
n-m-h3-prob-08.s.s3.hint.0: Find probability for each of the three ways the real match fit end, then check say dem add up to 1.
n-m-h3-prob-08.s.s3.hint.1: If dem play both remaining games, make table wey show who win championship for each of the four outcomes.
n-m-h3-prob-08.s.s3.o.a: Dem really go play two more games, so all four outcomes fit happen.
n-m-h3-prob-08.s.s3.r.a: This explanation contradict the fact say match dey end early. Dem no really play all the games.
n-m-h3-prob-08.s.s3.o.b: The number of games before the end gats be the same for prize sharing to fair.
n-m-h3-prob-08.s.s3.r.b: You base fairness on how many games before the end. The standard na probability of winning.
n-m-h3-prob-08.s.s3.o.c: Na just for convenience, so e no matter as long as the value correct.
n-m-h3-prob-08.s.s3.r.c: You no explain why the value correct. Reason dey why this way dey fine.
n-m-h3-prob-08.s.s3.o.d: Games after deciding the match no dey change the winning team, so result remain the same even if dem play all.
n-m-h3-prob-08.s.s3.explain: If A win the next game, A na champion, and games after that no go change the winner. So even if we assume say dem play both remaining games, "who win the championship" no change, and the four outcomes each get equal chance of 1/4, so counting easy. If we treat the three ways the real match fit end ("A win" with 1/2, "B win then A win" with 1/4, "B win twice one after another" with 1/4) as equal chance, that one wrong.

n-m-h3-serieslim-01.title: If We Group the Terms, Sum Still Be the Same?
n-m-h3-serieslim-01.topic: Series: partial sums and infinite geometric series
n-m-h3-serieslim-01.goal: Write the partial sums yourself, then check and explain why convergence of a series with grouped terms no mean say the original series converge.
n-m-h3-serieslim-01.material: Three friends dey argue about the sum of series 1−1+1−1+1−1+…. Information dey come out one piece at a time. (The general term na (−1)^(n−1): 1 if n odd, −1 if n even.)
n-m-h3-serieslim-01.thinking.1: Use partial sums to judge whether series converge
n-m-h3-serieslim-01.thinking.2: Sort out which direction hold between grouped series and original series
n-m-h3-serieslim-01.prereq.1: Define sum of a series as the limit of its partial sums
n-m-h3-serieslim-01.s.s1.prompt: At each stage, make judgment using only wetin you know by then.
n-m-h3-serieslim-01.s.s1.hint.0: When new information show, reconsider whether the judgment wey you choose just before still okay.
n-m-h3-serieslim-01.s.s1.hint.1: Write out two different groupings and compare whether the same value come out every time dem group the terms.
n-m-h3-serieslim-01.s.s1.st.0.info: Mina group the terms two at a time and write (1−1)+(1−1)+(1−1)+…, so each bracket na 0.
n-m-h3-serieslim-01.s.s1.st.0.ask: Wetin you think the sum of this series be?
n-m-h3-serieslim-01.s.s1.st.0.after: The grouping fit give 0 or 1, so you fit see say e too early to state the sum just because "I group am one way."
n-m-h3-serieslim-01.s.s1.st.0.o.a: E be 0: because every group na 0
n-m-h3-serieslim-01.s.s1.st.0.r.a: You accept the result of one grouping as the sum. Na the first judgment wey come mind.
n-m-h3-serieslim-01.s.s1.st.0.o.b: E be 1: because if we leave the first term 1 and group as 1+(−1+1)+(−1+1)+…, e give 1
n-m-h3-serieslim-01.s.s1.st.0.r.b: You try another grouping and get different value. But look well at how you decide straight away say that value na the sum.
n-m-h3-serieslim-01.s.s1.st.0.o.c: Too early to decide: we gats check whether the value remain the same when we change grouping
n-m-h3-serieslim-01.s.s1.st.0.r.c: You suspect say result fit change depending on how dem group the terms.
n-m-h3-serieslim-01.s.s1.st.1.info: Writing the partial sums in order give S_1=1, S_2=0, S_3=1, S_4=0, S_5=1, ….
n-m-h3-serieslim-01.s.s1.st.1.ask: Dem define a series by the limit of its partial sums. Now wetin you think?
n-m-h3-serieslim-01.s.s1.st.1.after: The partial sums no dey approach one single value, so this series diverge. Dem no determine the sum.
n-m-h3-serieslim-01.s.s1.st.1.o.a: E converge to 0: because S_2, S_4, … all na 0
n-m-h3-serieslim-01.s.s1.st.1.r.a: You look only at the even-numbered partial sums. You miss say the odd-numbered ones na 1.
n-m-h3-serieslim-01.s.s1.st.1.o.b: E converge to 1: because S_1, S_3, … all na 1
n-m-h3-serieslim-01.s.s1.st.1.r.b: You look only at the odd-numbered partial sums. You miss say the even-numbered ones na 0.
n-m-h3-serieslim-01.s.s1.st.1.o.c: E no converge: because the partial sums dey change between 0 and 1 and no dey approach one single value
n-m-h3-serieslim-01.s.s1.st.1.r.c: You look at how all the partial sums behave and judge according to the definition of limit.
n-m-h3-serieslim-01.s.s1.st.2.info: But the series 0+0+0+… wey Mina make by grouping clearly converge to 0.
n-m-h3-serieslim-01.s.s1.st.2.ask: From the fact say the grouped series converge, wetin we fit talk about the original series?
n-m-h3-serieslim-01.s.s1.st.2.after: If the original series converge, the grouped series go converge to the same value. But the reverse no hold, because the grouped series use only S_2, S_4, ….
n-m-h3-serieslim-01.s.s1.st.2.o.a: The original series too converge with the same sum: because we only group the terms
n-m-h3-serieslim-01.s.s1.st.2.r.a: You apply the idea say grouping keep the sum unchanged both ways.
n-m-h3-serieslim-01.s.s1.st.2.o.b: We no fit determine anything: because partial sums of the grouped series na only some of the original partial sums
n-m-h3-serieslim-01.s.s1.st.2.r.b: You point out say grouped series use only some of the original partial sums.
n-m-h3-serieslim-01.s.s1.st.2.o.c: The original series sum na both 0 and 1: because each grouping method get one sum
n-m-h3-serieslim-01.s.s1.st.2.r.c: You say a series wey no converge get two sums. A sum mean one limit of the partial sums.
n-m-h3-serieslim-01.s.s1.reflect: At first, calculation of 0 by grouping look reasonable, but your judgment change after you write partial sums. Whether series converge no depend on grouping; e depend on how all partial sums S_n behave.
n-m-h3-serieslim-01.s.s2.prompt: Soyoung talk, "Grouping with parentheses give 0+0+0+…, so sum of 1−1+1−1+… na 0." Write explanation for Soyoung. Include how partial sums of original series behave and how partial sums of grouped series relate to original ones.
n-m-h3-serieslim-01.s.s2.hint.0: First write S_1, S_2, S_3, S_4 yourself and note how values change.
n-m-h3-serieslim-01.s.s2.hint.1: Point out which original partial sums na the grouped series partial sums (1−1)+(1−1)+… .
n-m-h3-serieslim-01.s.s2.selfAssess.0: You really check values of partial sums S_1, S_2, S_3, S_4?
n-m-h3-serieslim-01.s.s2.selfAssess.1: You say which original partial sums grouped series dey use?
n-m-h3-serieslim-01.s.s2.selfAssess.2: You think whether "grouped series converge" guarantee say "original series converge"?
n-m-h3-serieslim-01.s.s2.model.0: Partial sums of original series na 1, 0, 1, 0, …, dey alternate between 0 and 1 and no approach one value. So e get no sum. Partial sums of grouped series pick only some of dem (the even-numbered ones), like S_2, S_4, …, so e just happen say dem come out as 0.
n-m-h3-serieslim-01.s.s2.model.1: Partial sums repeat 1,0,1,0 and no converge. If we change grouping to 1+(−1+1)+(−1+1)+…, e give 1, so value depend on grouping. Grouped series being 0 no tell anything about sum of original series.
n-m-h3-serieslim-01.s.s2.model.2: Soyoung, original series S_n na 1 when n odd and 0 when n even, so e get no limit (e diverge). Grouping with parentheses mean you only look at S_2, S_4, …, wey give 0; that no prove original series converge.

n-m-h3-serieslim-04.topic: Series: partial sums and infinite geometric series
n-m-h3-serieslim-04.title: 0.999… small pass 1?
n-m-h3-serieslim-04.goal: Explain using limit of a difference say limit fit be the sum even if partial sums never reach am, and build another series with same feature.
n-m-h3-serieslim-04.material: Two friends dey argue whether 0.999… (with 9 repeating forever) equal 1. Yuna: "0.9, 0.99, 0.999, … always below 1 however far you go, so 0.999… below 1." Dohyun: "0.999…=9/10+9/100+9/1000+…, an infinite geometric series with first term 9/10 and common ratio 1/10, so total na 1."
n-m-h3-serieslim-04.thinking.0: Check whether evidence support a claim conclusion
n-m-h3-serieslim-04.thinking.1: Tell apart partial sums and limits
n-m-h3-serieslim-04.s.s1.prompt: Look at both friends statements and evidence, then choose most suitable judgment.
n-m-h3-serieslim-04.s.s1.hint.0: Check separately whether Yuna evidence true and whether conclusion follow from am.
n-m-h3-serieslim-04.s.s1.hint.1: Write how sum of series defined, then compare whether Dohyun calculation match that definition.
n-m-h3-serieslim-04.s.s1.o.a: Dohyun correct: sum of series na limit of partial sums, and partial sums dey get close to 1 more and more
n-m-h3-serieslim-04.s.s1.r.a: You judge by definition of sum (limit of partial sums). You also see Yuna evidence no lead to her conclusion.
n-m-h3-serieslim-04.s.s1.o.b: Sum no determine: because partial sums keep changing forever and no fit get one value
n-m-h3-serieslim-04.s.s1.r.b: You mix up partial sums changing with not converging. Even if dem change, series converge if dem approach one value.
n-m-h3-serieslim-04.s.s1.o.c: Yuna correct: no partial sum equal 1, so 0.999… different from 1
n-m-h3-serieslim-04.s.s1.r.c: You carry property of every partial sum directly over to limit. Limit no be one of partial sums.
n-m-h3-serieslim-04.s.s1.o.d: Both correct: 0.999… below 1 by a tiny amount, but for calculation dem treat am as 1
n-m-h3-serieslim-04.s.s1.r.d: You say positive difference from 1 remain, but also say e equal 1. For real numbers, two values equal only if difference na 0.
n-m-h3-serieslim-04.s.s1.explain: Sum of series na limit of partial sums S_n. Here S_n=1−(1/10)^n and limit na 1, so 0.999…=1. Yuna evidence true, but "all S_n below 1" no mean "lim S_n below 1" (at limit e fit become ≤).
n-m-h3-serieslim-04.s.s2.prompt: Yuna statement "no matter how many terms you add, partial sum below 1" na true. But her conclusion wrong. Explain why using 1−S_n, the difference between 1 and partial sum S_n.
n-m-h3-serieslim-04.s.s2.hint.0: Write S_1, S_2, S_3 and each difference from 1.
n-m-h3-serieslim-04.s.s2.hint.1: Connect how that difference change as n grow with wetin define sum of series, as the limit of.
n-m-h3-serieslim-04.s.s2.selfAssess.0: You write 1−S_n as formula with n?
n-m-h3-serieslim-04.s.s2.selfAssess.1: You connect that value approaching 0 with total being 1?
n-m-h3-serieslim-04.s.s2.selfAssess.2: You say limit fit be 1 even though partial sums never reach 1?
n-m-h3-serieslim-04.s.s2.model.0: 1−S_n=1/10^n always bigger than 0, so true say S_n below 1. But as n grow, 1/10^n come arbitrarily close to 0, so limit of S_n na 1; since sum of series na that limit, 0.999…=1.
n-m-h3-serieslim-04.s.s2.model.1: No partial sum ever reach 1, but 1−S_n=(1/10)^n converge to 0. Sum of series na limit of partial sums, so e be 1. Even if every partial sum below 1, limit fit be 1.
n-m-h3-serieslim-04.s.s2.model.2: Every S_n below 1, but difference 0.00…01 dey get arbitrarily small as n grow, so limit na 1, and so 0.999…=1.
n-m-h3-serieslim-04.s.s3.prompt: Make series with same feature yourself. Enter two infinite geometric series a + ar + ar² + … with first term a and common ratio r, sum 1, and all partial sums below 1, using different common ratios. (You fit use decimals.)
n-m-h3-serieslim-04.s.s3.hint.0: First write equation between a and r wey must hold for sum to be 1.
n-m-h3-serieslim-04.s.s3.hint.1: Calculate S_1 and S_2 to check which sign r must get so all partial sums below 1.
n-m-h3-serieslim-04.s.s3.ok.c1: Absolute value of common ratio below 1, so e converge.
n-m-h3-serieslim-04.s.s3.fail.c1: |r|<1 no hold, so this no be convergent series with sum 1.
n-m-h3-serieslim-04.s.s3.ok.c3: All terms positive, so partial sums below 1.
n-m-h3-serieslim-04.s.s3.fail.c3: Common ratio no positive, so partial sum fit pass 1.
n-m-h3-serieslim-04.s.s3.explain: If a=1−r and 0<r<1, partial sum S_n=1−r^n always below 1 but its limit na 1. a=0.9, r=0.1 exactly give 0.999…. If r negative, a=1−r>1, so even first partial sum already pass 1.

n-m-h3-integc-08.title: Area of same region: two people, two different solutions

n-m-h3-integc-08.material: Two people find area of region R enclosed by curve y=ln x, x-axis, and line x=e using different methods. (∫_1^e na definite integral from 1 to e.)

n-m-h3-integc-08.s.s1.explain: Rectangle area for 0≤x≤e, 0≤y≤1 na e. At each height y, point on curve na x=eʸ, so width of part to its left na eʸ, and area na ∫_0^1 eʸ dy = e−1. R dey to right of curve, so area na e−(e−1)=1.

n-m-h3-vec-04.title: Angle between two lines same as angle between their direction vectors?
n-m-h3-vec-04.goal: Understand difference between angle between direction vectors and angle between lines by updating your judgment when information come out, then use correct formula for angle between lines.
n-m-h3-vec-04.material: You want find angle θ between two lines l and m on coordinate plane. Information dey come out one piece at a time. (u·v read "u dot v," |u| na magnitude of u, and √5 read "root 5.")
n-m-h3-vec-04.thinking.0: Update judgment when new information show
n-m-h3-vec-04.thinking.1: Check whether value stay same if direction vector chosen differently
n-m-h3-vec-04.prereq.0: Dot product of plane vectors and angle between dem
n-m-h3-vec-04.s.s1.prompt: Information dey come out one piece at a time. At each step, choose judgment using only wetin you know up to then.
n-m-h3-vec-04.s.s1.hint.0: Each time new information show, check whether your earlier judgment still hold.
n-m-h3-vec-04.s.s1.hint.1: For same line, choose direction vector pointing opposite way, do same calculation, and compare results.
n-m-h3-vec-04.s.s1.st.0.info: You choose u=(1, 2) as direction vector for line l and v=(1, −3) as direction vector for line m. Calculation give u·v=−5, |u|=√5, |v|=√10.
n-m-h3-vec-04.s.s1.st.0.ask: How you judge angle θ between the two lines?
n-m-h3-vec-04.s.s1.st.0.after: Angle between u and v get cos = −1/√2, that is, 135°. But nobody don confirm yet whether this fit be angle between lines.
n-m-h3-vec-04.s.s1.st.0.r.a: You transfer angle between two vectors directly to angle between lines. Na the first judgment wey come mind.
n-m-h3-vec-04.s.s1.st.0.o.b: We need check more whether this value really describe angle between lines, and whether e remain the same if direction vectors chosen differently
n-m-h3-vec-04.s.s1.st.0.r.b: You remember say one line no get only one fixed direction vector.
n-m-h3-vec-04.s.s1.st.0.o.c: Since dot product negative, all we fit talk na say the two lines no perpendicular
n-m-h3-vec-04.s.s1.st.0.r.c: You only talk say dem no perpendicular. You no find the angle size.
n-m-h3-vec-04.s.s1.st.1.info: Even if you use −v=(−1, 3) as direction vector of line m instead of v, e still be the same line m.
n-m-h3-vec-04.s.s1.st.1.ask: Wetin be angle between u and −v, and wetin e tell us about angle θ between the lines?
n-m-h3-vec-04.s.s1.st.1.after: Angle between u and v na 135°, and between u and −v na 45°. Even for the same two lines, the value change depending on how dem choose direction vector. When two lines meet, angles 45° and 135° form, so we need one rule to decide which one to call angle between the lines.
n-m-h3-vec-04.s.s1.st.1.o.a: u·(−v)=5 and cos=1/√2, so angle na 45°. For the same lines, angles 135° and 45° both come out, so signed dot product alone no determine angle between lines.
n-m-h3-vec-04.s.s1.st.1.r.a: You check directly say value dey change depending on how dem choose direction vector.
n-m-h3-vec-04.s.s1.st.1.r.b: Changing to −v change sign of dot product, so cos become +1/√2; this no be mistake.
n-m-h3-vec-04.s.s1.st.1.o.c: u·(−v)=5 and angle na 45°, so earlier 135° wrong and angle between lines na 45°
n-m-h3-vec-04.s.s1.st.1.r.c: You correct say 45° come out, but you miss say both 135° and 45° come from same two lines. We need rule for which one to use as angle between the lines.
n-m-h3-vec-04.s.s1.st.2.info: We agree say angle θ between two lines na the smaller of the two angle types wey form where dem meet (45° and 135°), that is, 0°<θ≤90°.
n-m-h3-vec-04.s.s1.st.2.ask: Which formula go always give θ no matter how dem choose direction vectors?
n-m-h3-vec-04.s.s1.st.2.after: |u·v|=5, so cosθ=5/(√5·√10)=1/√2 and θ=45°. To find angle between lines, formula gats use absolute value of dot product, so same value go come out regardless of direction vectors.
n-m-h3-vec-04.s.s1.st.2.r.a: The sign dey change depending on direction vector choice, so e fit no match the rule say θ dey between 0° and 90°.
n-m-h3-vec-04.s.s1.st.2.r.b: Using absolute value of dot product give same value even if direction vector turn around, and cosθ≥0, so θ no pass 90°.
n-m-h3-vec-04.s.s1.st.2.r.c: This correct only when dem use −v; if dem choose the other way, sign different, so this no be formula wey always correct.
n-m-h3-vec-04.s.s1.reflect: At first you transfer angle between direction vectors straight to angle between lines, but your judgment change when information say same line get direction vectors for two opposite directions. Angle between lines gats be quantity wey no change with direction vector sign, so we find am by using absolute value of dot product.
n-m-h3-vec-04.s.s2.prompt: Direction vector of line p na (2, 1), and direction vector of line q na (1, −3). Find cosθ for angle θ between the lines, and write one sentence why formula need absolute value.

n-m-h3-vec-04.s.s2.selfAssess.1: You compare the angle wey come out if you use dot product directly when e negative?
n-m-h3-vec-04.s.s2.selfAssess.2: You connect reason for absolute value to "how dem choose direction vector"?
n-m-h3-vec-04.s.s2.model.0: (2, 1)·(1, −3)=−1 and sizes na √5 and √10, so cosθ=|−1|/(√5·√10)=1/(5√2)≈0.14. If we reverse direction vector, dot product sign change, so absolute value dey needed to get one definite angle between lines.
n-m-h3-vec-04.s.s2.model.1: Dot product na −1 and |p|=√5, |q|=√10, so cosθ=1/√50=√2/10. We use absolute value because we agree say angle between lines no pass 90°, and we want the same value however dem choose direction vectors.

n-m-h3-dist-06.title: If You Toss Coin Many Times, Half Go Show Exactly?
n-m-h3-dist-06.topic: Probability distributions: binomial distribution and number of trials
n-m-h3-dist-06.goal: Check step by step how probability of "exactly half" and probability of "near half" change differently as number of trials grow, then revise your first idea.
n-m-h3-dist-06.material: Make X the number of heads when dem toss fair coin. Dem reveal information one piece at a time. (Calculator find probabilities for plenty tosses.)
n-m-h3-dist-06.thinking.1: Tell apart probability of exact value from probability of a range

n-m-h3-dist-06.s.s1.st.0.ask: About how likely you think say exactly 5 heads go show?
n-m-h3-dist-06.s.s1.st.0.after: C(10,5)/2¹⁰=252/1024≈0.246. Even though na the most likely count, probability na only about 25%.
n-m-h3-dist-06.s.s1.st.0.o.a: About 50%: because exactly half na the most natural result
n-m-h3-dist-06.s.s1.st.0.r.a: You think say getting half na the most natural result, so probability suppose be 50%.
n-m-h3-dist-06.s.s1.st.0.o.b: About 25%: because na the middle count, but e share probability with nearby counts like 4 and 6
n-m-h3-dist-06.s.s1.st.0.r.b: You notice say even the most likely middle count share probability with nearby counts.
n-m-h3-dist-06.s.s1.st.0.o.c: Below 5%: because e rare to get exactly that number
n-m-h3-dist-06.s.s1.st.0.r.c: You think say e very rare to get exactly that count.

n-m-h3-dist-06.s.s1.st.1.ask: How e compare with about 25% for 10 tosses?
n-m-h3-dist-06.s.s1.st.1.after: C(100,50)/2¹⁰⁰≈0.080. As number of tosses grow, probability of "exactly half" really dey get smaller.
n-m-h3-dist-06.s.s1.st.1.o.a: E dey get smaller: because plenty more nearby counts get similar probability
n-m-h3-dist-06.s.s1.st.1.r.a: You see say more nearby counts get probability like the middle count, so share for the one middle value dey shrink.
n-m-h3-dist-06.s.s1.st.1.o.b: E dey get bigger: because the more you toss, the closer you dey get to half
n-m-h3-dist-06.s.s1.st.1.r.b: You think say the more tosses you do, exactly half go show.
n-m-h3-dist-06.s.s1.st.1.o.c: E dey around the same: because e still be half and half
n-m-h3-dist-06.s.s1.st.1.r.c: You only look say e be half and half, and miss how changed number of tosses affect am.
n-m-h3-dist-06.s.s1.st.2.info: Now question na probability say, for 100 tosses, proportion of heads dey between 40% and 60% inclusive (40 to 60 heads). For 10 tosses, probability of getting 4 to 6 heads na about 66%.
n-m-h3-dist-06.s.s1.st.2.ask: Wetin happen to this probability for 100 tosses?
n-m-h3-dist-06.s.s1.st.2.after: Probability of getting 40 to 60 heads na about 0.965. Probability of exactly 50 go down, but probability of getting near half really go up.
n-m-h3-dist-06.s.s1.st.2.o.a: Lower than 66%: because probability of exactly half too go down
n-m-h3-dist-06.s.s1.st.2.r.a: You think say since probability of exactly half reduce, probability near half must reduce too.
n-m-h3-dist-06.s.s1.st.2.o.b: About 8%: because probability for 100 tosses na 8%
n-m-h3-dist-06.s.s1.st.2.r.b: You mix up probability of exactly 50 with probability for a range.
n-m-h3-dist-06.s.s1.st.2.o.c: More than 90%: because results gather near half
n-m-h3-dist-06.s.s1.st.2.r.c: You look the combined probability for range near half, no be the exact value.
n-m-h3-dist-06.s.s1.reflect: At first, e easy to think say "the more tosses you do, the more exactly half go show." But as number of tosses grow, probability of exactly half dey go down, while probability say proportion of heads land near half dey go up. n-m-h3-serieslim-02.topic: Series: partial sums and infinite geometric series

n-m-h3-serieslim-02.goal: Learn say you must find a_1 separately when finding general term from partial sum S_n, correct wrong solution and check using sum lim S_n.
n-m-h3-serieslim-02.material: Sum of first n terms of series na S_n = 4 − 3·(1/2)^(n−1). Read Minjae solution for finding sum of this series. ((1/2)^(n−1) mean one-half to power n−1.)

n-m-h3-serieslim-06.goal: Make example of infinite geometric series wey sum na 6 but first term pass 6, and explain how common ratio sign make partial sums go above and below the sum.
n-m-h3-serieslim-06.material: Suppose infinite geometric series a + ar + ar² + … with first term a and common ratio r get sum 6. E easy to think, "The sum na 6, so first term gats less than 6."

n-m-h3-serieslim-06.s.s1.prompt: Make an infinite geometric series with sum 6 and first term a greater than 6, and choose n (natural number from 1 to 9) where partial sum S_n of that series greater than 6. Enter a, r, n. Make three examples with different (r, n). (S_n na sum from first term reach nth term.)
n-m-h3-serieslim-06.s.s1.hint.0: First write the equation between a and r wey make the sum 6.

For example, if a=9 and r=−1/2, S_1=9 and S_3=6(1+1/8)=6.75 pass 6, while S_2=4.5 less. r=−1 no allowed because |r|<1 fail, and a=8, r=−1/2 get sum 8/1.5≈5.33.

n-m-h3-serieslim-07.title: When Does Sum Series of Two Series Converge?
n-m-h3-serieslim-07.goal: Sort the combinations where convergence of Σ(a_n+b_n) dey decided by whether Σa_n and Σb_n converge, and where e no dey decided; then make counterexample.
n-m-h3-serieslim-07.material: Two infinite series Σa_n and Σb_n dey here, and you wan know whether series Σ(a_n+b_n), wey you make by adding terms one by one, converge or diverge. Depending on wetin you know, sometimes e dey clear and sometimes e no dey.

n-m-h3-serieslim-07.s.s1.prompt: Choose all information pieces wey determine one answer: whether Σ(a_n+b_n) converge or diverge.

n-m-h3-serieslim-07.s.s1.r.a: Sum of two convergent series converge, so the answer dey determined.
n-m-h3-serieslim-07.s.s1.r.b: If a_n=b_n=1 e diverge, but if a_n=1, b_n=−1 the sum series converge, so answer no dey determined.
n-m-h3-serieslim-07.s.s1.r.c: Removing convergent Σa_n from the sum leave Σb_n, so if the sum series converge, Σb_n too gats converge; so the sum series diverge.
n-m-h3-serieslim-07.s.s1.o.d: a_n and b_n both converge to 0
n-m-h3-serieslim-07.s.s1.r.d: If a_n=b_n=1/n, sum series diverge; if a_n=1/n², b_n=1/n², e converge. So e no dey determined.
n-m-h3-serieslim-07.s.s1.explain: If both converge, sum series converge; if only one converge, sum series diverge (because if e converge, Σb_n=Σ(a_n+b_n)−Σa_n too gats converge). If both diverge, or terms go to 0, that alone no determine am.
n-m-h3-serieslim-07.s.s2.prompt: Show one case where information no enough. Let a_n=p·r^n, b_n=q·r^n (p≠0, q≠0, |r|≥1); then both Σa_n and Σb_n diverge. Enter p, q, r two times, with different r, so Σ(a_n+b_n) converge.
n-m-h3-serieslim-07.s.s2.hint.0: Write a_n+b_n by grouping r^n, then think wetin coefficient gats be for the series to converge.
n-m-h3-serieslim-07.s.s2.hint.1: Find how to make coefficient 0 while keeping condition say neither p nor q na 0.
n-m-h3-serieslim-07.s.s2.ok.c1: The general terms of Σa_n and Σb_n no be 0, so each one diverge.
n-m-h3-serieslim-07.s.s2.fail.c1: p or q na 0, so that series no diverge.
n-m-h3-serieslim-07.s.s2.ok.c2: |r|≥1, so general term no dey go to 0, and each one diverge.
n-m-h3-serieslim-07.s.s2.fail.c3: (p+q)r^n no be 0, so sum series diverge too.
n-m-h3-serieslim-07.s.s2.explain: Since a_n+b_n=(p+q)r^n, if p+q=0 every term na 0, so sum series converge to 0. But if p≠0 and |r|≥1, a_n and b_n no dey go to 0, so both diverge. With p=q=1 the sum series too diverge; with |r|<1 each series converge.
n-m-h3-serieslim-07.s.s3.prompt: Explain why statement "if Σa_n and Σb_n both diverge, then Σ(a_n+b_n) too diverge" wrong. Use example from previous step, and write condition we need when we split sum series into two series.

n-m-h3-serieslim-07.s.s3.model.0: Even if both diverge, like Σa_n with p·r^n and Σb_n with −p·r^n, when dem add every term na 0, so e converge. So if both diverge, we no fit determine whether sum series converge. To split the sum into Σa_n+Σb_n, both gats converge.
n-m-h3-serieslim-07.s.s3.model.1: Counterexample dey. If a_n=2^n and b_n=−2^n, both diverge, but a_n+b_n=0, so sum series converge to 0. So Σ(a_n+b_n)=Σa_n+Σb_n fit use only when both series converge.
n-m-h3-serieslim-07.s.s3.model.2: Two divergent series fit converge when dem cancel (1 and −1 add reach 0), or diverge if dem get the same sign. So before splitting, first check say each series converge.

n-m-h3-diffc-06.s.s3.prompt: Rewrite sentence 3 so Haeun go understand. E suppose include wetin f″(x)>0 tell you and wetin decide whether f(x) dey increase or decrease.

n-m-h3-diffc-06.s.s3.model.0: If f″(x)>0, slope of tangent line dey get bigger and graph dey curve downward. But sign of f′(x) decide whether f(x) dey increase or decrease. For example, f(x)=x² get f″=2>0 when x<0, but f′=2x<0, so e dey decrease.
n-m-h3-diffc-06.s.s3.model.1: f″>0 mean f′ dey increase, that is, slope dey get bigger. Whether e dey go up to the right depend on whether slope positive, that is, whether f′>0. If slope negative but dey get bigger, e dey go down and still get f″>0.

n-m-h3-prob-04.thinking.1: Make some examples wey satisfy conditions
n-m-h3-prob-04.topic: Probability: conditional probability, independence/dependence, Bayesian reasoning, setting up sample space
n-m-h3-prob-04.title: Wearing glasses and joining a club: make a table of unrelated traits
n-m-h3-prob-04.goal: Make some 2×2 tables where two events independent, and check how to read independence as "rates within groups equal."
n-m-h3-prob-04.material: You go make table to count 60 students in one class by "whether dem wear glasses" and "whether dem join club."
n-m-h3-prob-04.thinking.0: Turn meaning of independence into table
n-m-h3-prob-04.s.s1.prompt: 60 students for one class divide by "wear glasses" and "join club." Which statement best describe what it mean for the two to be independent?
n-m-h3-prob-04.s.s1.hint.0: Think whether among only students wey wear glasses, proportion wey join club same as proportion wey join overall.
n-m-h3-prob-04.s.s1.hint.1: If dem independent, "knowing whether student wear glasses no change chance of joining" must hold. Compare whether each option talk about this.
n-m-h3-prob-04.s.s1.o.a: Number of students wey wear glasses equal number wey no wear.
n-m-h3-prob-04.s.s1.r.a: You read am as group sizes being equal. Independence concern rates inside groups, no be group sizes.
n-m-h3-prob-04.s.s1.o.b: Number of club members among students with glasses equal number of members among those without glasses.
n-m-h3-prob-04.s.s1.r.b: You compare headcounts. If two groups get different sizes, rates fit different even if headcounts equal.
n-m-h3-prob-04.s.s1.o.c: Proportion of club members among students with glasses equal proportion among those without glasses.
n-m-h3-prob-04.s.s1.o.d: Every student wey wear glasses join, and every student wey no wear glasses no join.
n-m-h3-prob-04.s.s1.r.d: You treat two traits wey always happen together as independent. Na the strongest dependence, where knowing one determine the other.
n-m-h3-prob-04.s.s1.explain: If proportion wey join among students with glasses equal proportion among those without glasses, then knowing whether student wear glasses no change chance of joining. That is, P(join|glasses)=P(join), wey mean the same as P(glasses∩join)=P(glasses)P(join).
n-m-h3-prob-04.s.s2.prompt: Make tables for 60 students. Let a = number wey wear glasses and join, b = glasses but no join, c = no glasses but join, d = no glasses and no join. All 4 numbers must be natural numbers at least 1 and sum 60; glasses and joining must be independent; and number wearing glasses must differ from number of club members. Enter 3 different tables.
n-m-h3-prob-04.s.s2.hint.0: First decide number of students with glasses, x, and number of club members, y. If dem independent, number a of students with glasses wey join must be x×y÷60.
n-m-h3-prob-04.s.s2.hint.1: Choose x and y so a be integer, then fill remaining b, c, d so total 60, and check membership rates of two groups equal.
n-m-h3-prob-04.s.s2.ok.c1: All 4 numbers natural numbers at least 1.
n-m-h3-prob-04.s.s2.fail.c1: a, b, c, d all must be natural numbers at least 1.
n-m-h3-prob-04.s.s2.fail.c2: The 4 numbers no add up to 60.
n-m-h3-prob-04.s.s2.fail.c3: Dem no independent. Compare club membership rate for students with glasses and students without.
n-m-h3-prob-04.s.s2.ok.c4: Number wearing glasses different from number of club members.
n-m-h3-prob-04.s.s2.fail.c4: Number wearing glasses equal number of club members.
n-m-h3-prob-04.s.s2.explain: (10,10,20,20): among 20 students with glasses, 10 join (1/2), and among 40 without, 20 join (1/2), so rates equal. For (5,15,10,30), both group rates 1/4; and for (12,18,12,18), both be 2/5. For (10,10,10,30), rate 1/2 with glasses but 1/4 without, so dem no independent. (15,15,15,15) independent, but number with glasses equal number of club members, so e break condition 4.
n-m-h3-prob-04.s.s2.because.prompt: Choose one table, find and write membership rate among students with glasses and those without, and explain why that show independence.
n-m-h3-prob-04.s.s2.because.hint.0: For your table, first write number of students with glasses and without, then divide each group's club-member number by group size.
n-m-h3-prob-04.s.s2.because.hint.1: Put the two rates side by side, compare whether dem equal, and connect that to meaning of independence.
n-m-h3-prob-04.s.s2.because.placeholder: e.g. Among students with glasses, club membership rate na ...
n-m-h3-prob-04.s.s2.because.selfAssess.0: For each group, you find rate by dividing number of club members by number of students in that group?
n-m-h3-prob-04.s.s2.because.selfAssess.1: You connect equal rates to idea say glasses no change chance of joining?
n-m-h3-prob-04.s.s2.because.model.0: Out of 20 students with glasses, 10 join, so rate na 1/2; out of 40 without glasses, 20 join, so rate still 1/2. Since two rates equal, knowing whether student wear glasses no change chance of joining, so dem independent.
n-m-h3-prob-04.s.s2.because.model.1: Both groups, people wey wear glasses and those wey no, get 50% membership rate. So whether student wear glasses no affect chance of joining, and we fit say dem independent.

n-m-h3-diffc-07.s.s1.prompt: Choose first wrong line in Seoyeon solution.
n-m-h3-diffc-07.title: Second derivative of curve wey parameter give
n-m-h3-diffc-07.topic: Differentiation: second derivative of function wey dem give with parameter
n-m-h3-diffc-07.goal: For curve wey parameter give, find and correct mistake for solution wey differentiate dy/dx again, then choose correct formula.
n-m-h3-diffc-07.material: Na Seoyeon solution be this for finding second derivative d²y/dx² at t=2 on curve x=t², y=t³−3t (t>0). (t² mean t squared and t³ mean t cubed.)
n-m-h3-diffc-07.thinking.0: Find the first wrong line for the solution
n-m-h3-diffc-07.thinking.1: Find the value again with correct method
n-m-h3-diffc-07.thinking.2: Compare how the expressions dey built to choose correct formula
n-m-h3-diffc-07.s.s1.hint.0: Confirm say dy/dx on line 2 na expression in t, then think how to write the process of differentiating am with respect to x using chain rule.
n-m-h3-diffc-07.s.s1.hint.1: Describe with words which derivative each line dey find, and test whether e follow properly from previous line with simple example like x=t², y=t³.
n-m-h3-diffc-07.s.s1.explain: Line 3 na the first wrong one. dy/dx na expression in t, so to differentiate am with respect to x, first differentiate am with respect to t, then divide by dx/dt. Differentiating y and x two times each and dividing no be that calculation. Line 4 just use result from line 3.
n-m-h3-diffc-07.s.s2.prompt: Use correct method to find d²y/dx² when t=2, and write how you find am.
n-m-h3-diffc-07.s.s2.hint.0: Make dy/dx simpler as expression in t, then differentiate that expression with respect to t.
n-m-h3-diffc-07.s.s2.hint.1: To differentiate with respect to x, use dx/dt to think wetin you must divide the derivative with respect to t by.
n-m-h3-diffc-07.s.s2.selfAssess.0: You first make dy/dx simpler as expression in t?
n-m-h3-diffc-07.s.s2.selfAssess.1: You differentiate that expression with respect to t, then divide by dx/dt?
n-m-h3-diffc-07.s.s2.selfAssess.2: You check by putting value 15/32 inside directly?
n-m-h3-diffc-07.s.s2.model.0: dy/dx=(3t²−3)/(2t)=(3/2)(t−1/t), and differentiating this with respect to t give (3/2)(1+1/t²). Divide am by dx/dt=2t to get d²y/dx². When t=2, (3/2)(5/4)=15/8, divide by 4, give 15/32.
n-m-h3-diffc-07.s.s2.model.1: d²y/dx²=(d/dt(dy/dx))÷(dx/dt). Putting t=2 inside d/dt{(3/2)(t−1/t)}=(3/2)(1+1/t²) give 15/8; dividing by dx/dt=4 give 15/32.
n-m-h3-diffc-07.s.s3.prompt: Choose the correct formula for finding d²y/dx² for curve wey parameter give.
n-m-h3-diffc-07.s.s3.hint.0: First write wetin d²y/dx² fit read as: "differentiate wetin with respect to wetin."
n-m-h3-diffc-07.s.s3.hint.1: Use chain rule to think wetin you must multiply or divide by to change differentiation with respect to t to differentiation with respect to x.
n-m-h3-diffc-07.s.s3.o.a: Divide y differentiated two times with respect to t by x differentiated two times with respect to t
n-m-h3-diffc-07.s.s3.r.a: Na the method Seoyeon use be this. The ratio of values differentiated twice with respect to t different from dy/dx differentiated with respect to x.
n-m-h3-diffc-07.s.s3.o.b: Divide dy/dx differentiated one time with respect to t by x differentiated one time with respect to t
n-m-h3-diffc-07.s.s3.r.b: This show the process of differentiating dy/dx with respect to x using chain rule.
n-m-h3-diffc-07.s.s3.o.c: Divide dy/dx differentiated one time with respect to t by x differentiated two times with respect to t
n-m-h3-diffc-07.s.s3.r.c: You put second derivative of x for denominator. To change to differentiation with respect to x, divide by dx/dt one time.
n-m-h3-diffc-07.s.s3.o.d: Divide dy/dx differentiated one time with respect to t by square of x differentiated one time with respect to t
n-m-h3-diffc-07.s.s3.r.d: You square the denominator. For chain rule, the only thing you divide by to change differentiation with respect to t to differentiation with respect to x na dx/dt, one time.
n-m-h3-diffc-07.s.s3.explain: d²y/dx²=d/dx(dy/dx)=[d/dt(dy/dx)]·(dt/dx)=[d/dt(dy/dx)]÷(dx/dt). When t=2, the formulas above give 6, 15/16, and 15/128, each different from the correct value 15/32.

n-m-h3-conic-03.topic: Conic sections: definitions and tangent lines of parabolas, ellipses, hyperbolas; connection between shapes and equations
n-m-h3-conic-03.title: How path of point P change when point F move?
n-m-h3-conic-03.goal: Use definitions to confirm say same construction, moving F change path into circle, ellipse, or hyperbola. Build habit of not carry conclusion from one case unchanged into another.
n-m-h3-conic-03.material: For plane, circle center O and radius 6, and point F. As point Q move on circle, let P be where perpendicular bisector of FQ meet line OQ. We go study shape P trace as Q move around circle and position of F change.
n-m-h3-conic-03.thinking.1: Find path using sum and difference of distances
n-m-h3-conic-03.thinking.2: Notice danger of generalizing from special case (F=O)
n-m-h3-conic-03.prereq.0: Definitions of ellipses and hyperbolas (sum and difference of distances)
n-m-h3-conic-03.prereq.1: Point on perpendicular bisector of segment get same distance from both endpoints
n-m-h3-conic-03.s.s1.prompt: Information come one piece at a time as F move. At each step, choose judgment based only on wetin you know.
n-m-h3-conic-03.s.s1.hint.0: Each time new information show, draw figure showing where P dey on segment OQ.
n-m-h3-conic-03.s.s1.hint.1: Use PF=PQ to check whether sum or difference of PO and PF simplify to constant.
n-m-h3-conic-03.s.s1.st.0.info: First consider case where F same point as center O. Point on perpendicular bisector of FQ same distance from F and Q, so PF=PQ. P dey line OQ.
n-m-h3-conic-03.s.s1.st.0.ask: As Q go around circle once, wetin shape P trace?
n-m-h3-conic-03.s.s1.st.0.after: If F=O, then PO=PQ and PO+PQ=OQ=6, so PO=3. P dey 3 away from O, so e trace circle radius 3.
n-m-h3-conic-03.s.s1.st.0.o.a: Circle with center O and radius 6
n-m-h3-conic-03.s.s1.st.0.r.a: You only restate circle wey Q trace. P no be Q; na point on perpendicular bisector of FQ.
n-m-h3-conic-03.s.s1.st.0.o.b: Circle with center O and radius 3
n-m-h3-conic-03.s.s1.st.0.r.b: You see say P stay fixed distance from O.
n-m-h3-conic-03.s.s1.st.0.o.c: Ellipse with O and some point as foci
n-m-h3-conic-03.s.s1.st.0.r.c: We never get 2 foci case. F and O na same point.
n-m-h3-conic-03.s.s1.st.0.r.d: As Q move, P also move.
n-m-h3-conic-03.s.s1.st.1.info: F don move to point inside circle, 4 away from O. PF=PQ still true. If you draw figure, P dey segment OQ (between O and Q).
n-m-h3-conic-03.s.s1.st.1.after: Since P dey segment OQ, PO+PF=PO+PQ=OQ=6. Sum of distances from points O and F constant 6, so na ellipse with foci O and F, major axis length 6.
n-m-h3-conic-03.s.s1.st.1.o.a: Still circle centered at O, because Q dey on circle.
n-m-h3-conic-03.s.s1.st.1.r.a: When F move away from O, PO no longer constant. You carry previous conclusion forward without changing am.
n-m-h3-conic-03.s.s1.st.1.o.b: Hyperbola where difference of distances from O and F constant
n-m-h3-conic-03.s.s1.st.2.o.a: Hyperbola where difference of distances from O and F constant
n-m-h3-conic-03.s.s1.st.1.r.b: You no check whether PO and PF need add or subtract. Use fact say P dey segment OQ.
n-m-h3-conic-03.s.s1.st.1.o.c: Ellipse with constant sum of distances from O and F
n-m-h3-conic-03.s.s1.st.1.r.c: You see sum constant, because PO+PF=PO+PQ=OQ.
n-m-h3-conic-03.s.s1.st.1.o.d: Parabola with points same distance from F and a line
n-m-h3-conic-03.s.s1.st.1.r.d: Equal distances connect F and Q (PF=PQ); e na distance to point Q, no be line.
n-m-h3-conic-03.s.s1.st.2.info: This time F move outside circle, 9 away from O. If you draw figure, P no dey segment OQ, but on extension of line OQ (on Q side or O side). PF=PQ still true.
n-m-h3-conic-03.s.s1.st.2.after: For extension for Q side, PO=OQ+PQ, so PO−PF=6, and for extension for O side, PF−PO=6. Any way, |PO−PF|=6 dey constant, so na hyperbola with foci O and F and transverse axis length 6 (OF=9>6).
n-m-h3-conic-03.s.s1.st.2.o.b: An ellipse wey get constant sum, like for inside case
n-m-h3-conic-03.s.s1.st.2.r.b: You carry the result from inside case over without change. If P no dey on segment OQ, PO+PQ no be OQ.
n-m-h3-conic-03.s.s1.st.2.o.c: A circle wey get center O
n-m-h3-conic-03.s.s1.st.2.r.c: Check whether PO dey constant. If F dey far from O, e no dey constant.
n-m-h3-conic-03.s.s1.st.2.r.d: The perpendicular bisector and line OQ meet for almost every Q.
n-m-h3-conic-03.s.s1.reflect: As F position change, the same construction give circle, ellipse, and hyperbola one after the other. E wrong to carry the inside result over without change go outside. Depending on whether point P dey on segment OQ or the extension, e change whether the sum or the difference between PO and PF dey constant.
n-m-h3-conic-03.s.s2.prompt: Explain why the locus of P dey different when F dey inside the circle and when F dey outside, using PO, PF, and the circle radius 6.
n-m-h3-conic-03.s.s2.hint.0: Talk where P dey on line OQ for inside case and outside case.
n-m-h3-conic-03.s.s2.hint.1: For each case, connect how PO relate to PQ with the length 6.
n-m-h3-conic-03.s.s2.selfAssess.0: You write say PO+PF=6 inside and |PO−PF|=6 outside?
n-m-h3-conic-03.s.s2.selfAssess.1: You explain say the sum and difference split because P position (on the segment or on the extension) dey different?
n-m-h3-conic-03.s.s2.model.0: If F dey inside, P dey on segment OQ, so PO+PF=PO+PQ=6; the sum dey constant, and na ellipse. If F dey outside, P dey on the extension, so the difference between PO and PQ na 6; the difference between PO and PF dey constant 6, and na hyperbola.
n-m-h3-conic-03.s.s2.model.1: If F dey inside the circle, the sum of distances from O and F na 6, so na ellipse; if F dey outside the circle, the absolute difference between the distances dey constant 6, so na hyperbola. Na because whether P dey on the segment or on the extension dey change.

n-m-h3-conic-06.topic: Conic sections: definitions and tangent lines of parabolas, ellipses, hyperbolas; connection between shapes and equations
n-m-h3-conic-06.title: Where the focus and directrix go when dem shift parabola?
n-m-h3-conic-06.goal: Read the direction of a translation correctly from the equation, move the focus and directrix with the same translation, and write explanation for younger student.
n-m-h3-conic-06.material: Your junior Haeun send you note as e dey try find the focus and directrix of parabola (y−1)² = −8(x+2).
n-m-h3-conic-06.thinking.0: Reading how the signs for the equation match the shift direction
n-m-h3-conic-06.thinking.2: Rewriting the explanation to fit the person wey you dey explain to
n-m-h3-conic-06.prereq.0: The focus and directrix of parabola y²=4px
n-m-h3-conic-06.prereq.1: Translations and how the equation change
n-m-h3-conic-06.s.s1.prompt: Na the note your junior Haeun send be this. Choose the first line wey get mistake.
n-m-h3-conic-06.s.s1.hint.0: First find the point for the new equation where both sides equal 0. Compare am with where that role dey for the old one.
n-m-h3-conic-06.s.s1.hint.1: Tell the difference between whether each line calculation follow from the line before am or e be new judgment.
n-m-h3-conic-06.s.s1.line.0: For y² = −8x, 4p = −8, so p = −2, the focus na (−2, 0), and the directrix na x = 2.
n-m-h3-conic-06.s.s1.line.1: (y−1)² = −8(x+2) get x+2 and y−1, so e be y² = −8x shifted +2 along x direction and −1 along y direction.
n-m-h3-conic-06.s.s1.line.2: Moving the focus the same way give (−2+2, 0−1) = (0, −1).
n-m-h3-conic-06.s.s1.line.3: Moving the directrix the same way give x = 2+2 = 4.
n-m-h3-conic-06.s.s1.line.4: So the focus na (0, −1) and the directrix na x = 4.
n-m-h3-conic-06.s.s1.explain: Na line 2. Putting x+2 instead of x shift am −2 along x direction, and putting y−1 shift am +1 along y direction. The signs dey opposite. Everything from line 3 go down na calculation from the direction for line 2, so if the direction wrong, all of am wrong. Line 1 correct.
n-m-h3-conic-06.s.s2.prompt: Choose the most reliable way to check whether Haeun direction of translation correct.
n-m-h3-conic-06.s.s2.hint.0: Think about the feature wey the point matching the old vertex get for the new equation of the shifted figure.
n-m-h3-conic-06.s.s2.hint.1: First remember whether the focus and directrix dey on the curve.
n-m-h3-conic-06.s.s2.o.a: Put the focus wey dem find, (0, −1), inside to see whether e satisfy the new equation (y−1)² = −8(x+2).
n-m-h3-conic-06.s.s2.r.a: The focus no be point on the curve, so e no need satisfy the equation when you put am inside. So this check no fit tell you the translation direction.
n-m-h3-conic-06.s.s2.o.b: Compare whether coefficient −8 for the new equation na the same as the coefficient for the original equation.
n-m-h3-conic-06.s.s2.r.b: The coefficient only tell you the shape (the direction e open and the width). E no tell you which way the position shift.
n-m-h3-conic-06.s.s2.o.c: Find the point where both sides of the new equation equal 0, and see whether na where the old vertex (0, 0) move go.
n-m-h3-conic-06.s.s2.o.d: Draw the graph roughly and see whether the direction e open na the same as before.
n-m-h3-conic-06.s.s2.r.d: Translation no change the direction e open, so e go look the same even if the translation direction wrong.
n-m-h3-conic-06.s.s2.explain: The vertex na point (0, 0), where both sides of the old equation equal 0; so point (−2, 1), where both sides of the new equation equal 0, na where the vertex move go. So the translation na −2 along x-axis and +1 along y-axis. The focus and directrix no be points on the curve, so you no fit check dem by putting dem inside the equation.

n-m-h3-diffc-01.title: How we go read slope wey denominator be 0?
n-m-h3-diffc-01.topic: Differentiation: implicit differentiation and tangent lines at points where slope no dey defined
n-m-h3-diffc-01.goal: Check whether tangent line dey at point where denominator of slope from implicit differentiation be 0, then find and correct wrong conclusion in solution.
n-m-h3-diffc-01.material: Na Hayoon solution be this for finding tangent line at point P(2, −1) on curve C: x²+xy+y²=3. (x² and y² mean x squared and y squared. Dem check say point P dey on C with 4−2+1=3.)
n-m-h3-diffc-01.thinking.0: Find the wrong line for the solution
n-m-h3-diffc-01.thinking.1: Understand tangent line with undefined slope as shape of the graph
n-m-h3-diffc-01.thinking.2: Choose conditions to check before you conclude
n-m-h3-diffc-01.prereq.0: Implicit differentiation (treat y as function of x and differentiate both sides with respect to x)
n-m-h3-diffc-01.prereq.1: Find equation of tangent line at point on curve
n-m-h3-diffc-01.s.s1.prompt: Choose the first wrong line in Hayoon solution.
n-m-h3-diffc-01.s.s1.hint.0: Read each line from the top and calculate directly whether e follow from the line just before am.
n-m-h3-diffc-01.s.s1.hint.1: Compare whether the final conclusion dey say the same thing as the fact from the earlier line (wetin no dey defined).
n-m-h3-diffc-01.s.s1.line.0: Differentiate both sides with respect to x give 2x + (y + x·y′) + 2y·y′ = 0.
n-m-h3-diffc-01.s.s1.line.1: Solving for y′ give y′ = −(2x + y)/(x + 2y).
n-m-h3-diffc-01.s.s1.line.2: Put P(2, −1) inside, denominator x+2y na 2+2·(−1)=0, so slope no dey defined.
n-m-h3-diffc-01.s.s1.line.3: So no tangent line dey at point P.
n-m-h3-diffc-01.s.s1.explain: Line 4 wrong. Calculations for lines 1 to 3 correct. But "slope expression no dey defined" mean "no number wey be the slope," e no mean no tangent line dey. Numerator 2x+y=3 no be 0, so slope fit grow without limit, meaning tangent line parallel to y-axis fit dey.
n-m-h3-diffc-01.s.s2.prompt: If tangent line dey to curve C at point P, write the equation and the reason you decide so.
n-m-h3-diffc-01.s.s2.hint.0: Calculate what value the numerator get when denominator be 0, and think how big the slope become.
n-m-h3-diffc-01.s.s2.hint.1: Draw what line with slope wey dey grow without limit look like on coordinate plane, and write equation for that line through point P.
n-m-h3-diffc-01.s.s2.placeholder: e.g. Looking at direction of tangent line ...
n-m-h3-diffc-01.s.s2.selfAssess.0: You check say denominator be 0 but numerator no be 0?
n-m-h3-diffc-01.s.s2.selfAssess.1: You put x=2 inside curve equation and check how curve and line meet?
n-m-h3-diffc-01.s.s2.selfAssess.2: You fit explain difference between "no slope dey" and "no tangent line dey"?
n-m-h3-diffc-01.s.s2.model.0: Denominator be 0 and numerator be 3, so slope dey grow without limit. So tangent line na x=2, parallel to y-axis. Put x=2 inside curve give y²+2y+1=0, so y=−1 na the only solution; that mean the line just touch curve at point P, and that also make sense.
n-m-h3-diffc-01.s.s2.model.1: Tangent line dey. Slope no dey defined because tangent line vertical, and the equation na x=2. I also check say numerator 2x+y na 3, no be 0, so e no be form 0/0.
n-m-h3-diffc-01.s.s2.modelNote.1: E enough to check the numerator, even without using method wey put x=2 inside the curve.
n-m-h3-diffc-01.s.s3.prompt: Wetin you must check before you conclude "vertical tangent line dey" at point where denominator of slope expression be 0?
n-m-h3-diffc-01.s.s3.hint.0: For form y′ = (numerator)/(denominator), compare how fraction look different when denominator be 0 and numerator value no be the same.
n-m-h3-diffc-01.s.s3.hint.1: Form 0/0 and 3/0 na the same situation? Think wetin each one dey tell you.
n-m-h3-diffc-01.s.s3.o.a: Whether numerator still dey nonzero when denominator be 0 (that mean, whether e no be form 0/0)
n-m-h3-diffc-01.s.s3.r.a: You think say you should check numerator too.
n-m-h3-diffc-01.s.s3.o.b: Whether y value no be negative when point dey on curve
n-m-h3-diffc-01.s.s3.r.b: The sign of y no get anything to do with whether tangent line dey. You fit mix sign of coordinate with tangent direction.
n-m-h3-diffc-01.s.s3.o.c: Whether twice-differentiated value y″ no be 0
n-m-h3-diffc-01.s.s3.r.c: Second derivative only tell how the curve bend; e no decide whether tangent line dey.
n-m-h3-diffc-01.s.s3.o.d: Whether you fit write the curve as y = (expression in x)
n-m-h3-diffc-01.s.s3.r.d: Tangent line fit dey even if you no fit write implicit function as y=f(x). You no need this condition.
n-m-h3-diffc-01.s.s3.explain: Even if denominator be 0, if numerator no be 0, slope dey grow without limit and vertical tangent line show. If numerator too be 0, na form 0/0, so this expression alone no fit decide am; you must use another method to look the curve shape at that point.

n-m-h3-diffc-02.title: When velocity be 0, the point turn back?
n-m-h3-diffc-02.topic: Differentiation: velocity and acceleration, conditions for change of direction
n-m-h3-diffc-02.goal: Understand from velocity sign change the difference between when velocity be 0 and when direction of movement change, then build and check velocity expressions wey meet the conditions yourself.
n-m-h3-diffc-02.material: Velocity of point P moving on number line at time t (t≥0) na v(t), and v(1)=0. Minsu talk say, "When velocity be 0, the point must change direction." (Change direction mean e move from right to left or left to right. If velocity positive, e move right; if negative, e move left.)
n-m-h3-diffc-02.thinking.0: Choose the exact condition for change of direction
n-m-h3-diffc-02.thinking.1: Build and check velocity expressions wey satisfy the conditions
n-m-h3-diffc-02.thinking.2: Sort out wetin you fit judge from velocity and acceleration values alone
n-m-h3-diffc-02.prereq.0: How position, velocity, and acceleration relate (velocity na derivative of position, acceleration na derivative of velocity)
n-m-h3-diffc-02.prereq.1: How velocity sign relate to direction of movement
n-m-h3-diffc-02.prereq.2: Sign changes of a factored expression
n-m-h3-diffc-02.s.s1.prompt: Choose statement wey mean the same as "point P change direction at time t₀."
n-m-h3-diffc-02.s.s1.hint.0: First write which direction the point move when velocity positive and when e negative.
n-m-h3-diffc-02.s.s1.hint.1: Think what velocity sign must do for direction to change, and compare with when e become 0 then return to the same sign.
n-m-h3-diffc-02.s.s1.r.a: Even if acceleration no be 0, if velocity no be 0, direction stay the same. You fit mix velocity with acceleration.
n-m-h3-diffc-02.s.s1.o.b: Position at t₀ greater than positions for all times just before and after am
n-m-h3-diffc-02.s.s1.r.b: This only consider when position reach the highest point (right end). E leave out when e turn back at the left end.
n-m-h3-diffc-02.s.s1.r.c: v(t₀)=0 na only one feature of the moment direction change; e no be the same statement. Think about when v=0 but the sign stay the same.
n-m-h3-diffc-02.s.s1.o.d: Velocity signs just before and just after t₀ dey different
n-m-h3-diffc-02.s.s1.r.d: You see the direction change from the velocity sign change.
n-m-h3-diffc-02.s.s1.explain: Direction change when velocity sign change from positive to negative or negative to positive. Velocity being 0 na necessary condition wey happen when sign change, but e no enough by itself.
n-m-h3-diffc-02.s.s2.prompt: When velocity na v(t)=(t−1)^m (t−p)^n, enter at least 2 different triples (m, n, p) wey satisfy all these: point P no change direction at t=1, but e change direction at t=p. (m and n natural numbers from 1 to 6, p natural number from 2 to 9.)
n-m-h3-diffc-02.s.s2.hint.0: Try different m and n values and make table of signs of (t−1)^m and (t−p)^n just before and after t=1 and t=p.
n-m-h3-diffc-02.s.s2.hint.1: Split cases where exponent even or odd, and compare whether sign same or different just before and after that point.
n-m-h3-diffc-02.s.s2.ok.c1: m, n, and p na natural numbers within the ranges.
n-m-h3-diffc-02.s.s2.fail.c1: Dem must be natural numbers with 1≤m≤6, 1≤n≤6, 2≤p≤9.
n-m-h3-diffc-02.s.s2.ok.c2: Velocity sign dey the same just before and after t=1.
n-m-h3-diffc-02.s.s2.fail.c2: Velocity sign change just before and after t=1, so the point change direction.
n-m-h3-diffc-02.s.s2.ok.c3: Velocity sign dey different just before and after t=p.
n-m-h3-diffc-02.s.s2.fail.c3: Velocity sign dey the same just before and after t=p, so the point no change direction.
n-m-h3-diffc-02.s.s2.explain: If exponent for (t−1) even, this factor get same sign just before and after t=1; if exponent for (t−p) odd, the sign different just before and after t=p. The other factors no change sign near that point (p≥2). For (1, 1, 3), sign too change at t=1, and for (2, 2, 3), e no change at t=3.
n-m-h3-diffc-02.s.s2.because.prompt: Choose one example you find and write why the point no change direction at t=1 even though v(1)=0.
n-m-h3-diffc-02.s.s2.because.hint.0: Write v(t) with your chosen (m, n, p), then compare the signs when you put value a little below 1 and a little above 1.
n-m-h3-diffc-02.s.s2.because.hint.1: Connect whether (t−1)^m positive or negative just before and after t=1 to whether m be odd or even.
n-m-h3-diffc-02.s.s2.because.placeholder: e.g. Just before and after t=1, the sign of (t−1)^m be ...
n-m-h3-diffc-02.s.s2.because.selfAssess.0: For your chosen example, you really work out velocity sign before and after t=1?
n-m-h3-diffc-02.s.s2.because.selfAssess.1: You compare with the case where exponent odd?
n-m-h3-diffc-02.s.s2.because.model.0: I choose (2, 1, 3). For v=(t−1)²(t−3), (t−1)² dey at least 0 on both sides of t=1, so the sign no change; and (t−3) stay negative. So v be 0 at t=1 but the sign stay the same, and direction no change.
n-m-h3-diffc-02.s.s2.because.model.1: Exponent m even, so (t−1)^m no turn less than 0 as t pass 1. Velocity touch 0 then come back with same sign, so direction stay same.
n-m-h3-diffc-02.s.s2.because.modelNote.1: E include both the even exponent and the fact say the sign no change.
n-m-h3-diffc-02.s.s3.prompt: When velocity v be differentiable function and acceleration a(t)=v′(t), choose all correct statements.
n-m-h3-diffc-02.s.s3.hint.0: Make simple velocity expressions yourself, like v=(t−1)² and v=(t−1)³, calculate v′(1) for each, and compare with whether direction change.
n-m-h3-diffc-02.s.s3.hint.1: For each statement, find one counterexample to check whether e hold "always."
n-m-h3-diffc-02.s.s3.o.a: If v(t₀)=0 and a(t₀)≠0, the point change direction at t₀
n-m-h3-diffc-02.s.s3.r.a: You think say if acceleration no be 0, velocity graph pass through 0 and the sign change.
n-m-h3-diffc-02.s.s3.o.b: If v(t₀)=0 and a(t₀)=0, the point no change direction at t₀
n-m-h3-diffc-02.s.s3.r.b: Even if a(t₀)=0, for case like v=(t−1)³ direction change. You miss say when acceleration be 0, that alone no fit decide am.
n-m-h3-diffc-02.s.s3.o.c: If v(t₀)=0 and a(t₀)=0, the point must change direction at t₀
n-m-h3-diffc-02.s.s3.r.c: Even if a(t₀)=0, for case like v=(t−1)² direction stay the same.
n-m-h3-diffc-02.s.s3.o.d: If the point change direction at t₀, then v(t₀)=0 must be true
n-m-h3-diffc-02.s.s3.r.d: You think say for direction to change, velocity must change continuously and pass through 0.
n-m-h3-diffc-02.s.s3.explain: If v(t₀)=0 and v′(t₀)=a(t₀)≠0, then v pass through 0 and change sign. But if a(t₀)=0, sign fit stay the same like (t−1)² or change like (t−1)³, so you must look the velocity sign directly. For direction to change, continuous v must change sign, so v=0 at that moment.

n-m-h3-diffc-03.title: We fit find slope of composite function from values in table?
n-m-h3-diffc-03.topic: Differentiation: derivative of composite function and tables of function and derivative values
n-m-h3-diffc-03.goal: When finding derivative of composite function, decide which point to read outer function derivative from, and sort out wetin table values alone fit tell you.
n-m-h3-diffc-03.material:
Values of two differentiable functions f and g dey for table below. Values wey no dey in table no dey known. (f∘g)(x) mean f(g(x)), and (g∘f)(x) mean g(f(x)).
 x=1: f(1)=3, f′(1)=4, g(1)=2, g′(1)=−3
 x=2: f(2)=5, f′(2)=7, g(2)=1, g′(2)=6
n-m-h3-diffc-03.thinking.0: Sort out the values wey you need
n-m-h3-diffc-03.thinking.1: Tell apart wetin you fit find and wetin you no fit
n-m-h3-diffc-03.prereq.1: Read the table to find function values
n-m-h3-diffc-03.s.s1.prompt: Choose all values used to find (f∘g)′(1).
n-m-h3-diffc-03.s.s1.hint.0: Write derivative of composite function f(g(x)) as product of outer part and inner part, then look which value outer part use as input.
n-m-h3-diffc-03.s.s1.hint.1: Use the fact say when x=1, result of putting 1 inside g become input for f, to decide which table entries to read.
n-m-h3-diffc-03.s.s1.r.a: You read slope of f at x=1. Outer function f must use its slope at the value of inner function, g(1).
n-m-h3-diffc-03.s.s1.r.b: You read outer function derivative at the value of inner function, g(1).
n-m-h3-diffc-03.s.s1.r.c: g(1) needed to choose where differentiate outer function.
n-m-h3-diffc-03.s.s1.r.d: You remember multiply by inner function derivative too.
n-m-h3-diffc-03.s.s1.r.e: g′(2) na slope at x=2, so no use for answer at x=1.
n-m-h3-diffc-03.s.s1.r.f: f(2) na height, no be slope, so no use in derivative calculation.
n-m-h3-diffc-03.s.s1.explain: (f∘g)′(1)=f′(g(1))·g′(1). Since g(1)=2, use f′(2)=7 and multiply g′(1)=−3 to get −21. Key na use f′(g(1)), no be f′(1).
n-m-h3-diffc-03.s.s1.acc.0: g(1)=2 choose where to read f′; e no enter multiplication directly, but multiply f′(2) by g′(1) same calculation.
n-m-h3-diffc-03.s.s2.prompt: Choose all values wey table alone determine.
n-m-h3-diffc-03.s.s2.hint.0: For each composite, first find inner function value.
n-m-h3-diffc-03.s.s2.hint.1: Check if outer derivative at that input dey in table.
n-m-h3-diffc-03.s.s2.r.a: We need g′(3) at g(f(1))=g(3), but table no get am. Using g′(1) from table use different input.
n-m-h3-diffc-03.s.s2.r.b: Outer f slope f′(2) at input g(1)=2 dey in table.
n-m-h3-diffc-03.s.s2.r.c: Need g′(5) at g(f(2))=g(5), but table no get am.
n-m-h3-diffc-03.s.s2.r.d: Outer slope f′(1) at input g(2)=1 dey in table.
n-m-h3-diffc-03.s.s2.explain: To find composite derivative, table must show outer slope at inner function value. For (f∘g)′, g values 2 and 1 are listed x inputs, so can find. For (g∘f)′, f values 3 and 5 no dey as table inputs.
n-m-h3-diffc-03.s.s3.prompt: Find (f∘g)′(2), and explain why f′(2)·g′(2)=42 wrong.
n-m-h3-diffc-03.s.s3.hint.0: Read g(2) from table first and choose point to differentiate outer function.
n-m-h3-diffc-03.s.s3.hint.1: In calculation giving 42, compare where you read f derivative with actual input to f.
n-m-h3-diffc-03.s.s3.selfAssess.0: You first find g(2) and choose where read outer function?
n-m-h3-diffc-03.s.s3.selfAssess.1: You say which point slope got mixed into 42?
n-m-h3-diffc-03.s.s3.model.0: g(2)=1, so read f′ at 1: (f∘g)′(2)=f′(1)·g′(2)=4×6=24. f′(2)·g′(2)=42 use f slope at x=2, but input to f na g(2)=1, so wrong. The incorrect expression uses x=2.
n-m-h3-diffc-03.s.s3.model.1: Composite derivative na f′(g(2))g′(2). Since g(2)=1, f′(1)=4, g′(2)=6, product 24. 42 wrong because e use f′(2)=7.

n-m-h3-dist-02.title: When we fit call am binomial distribution if we draw 3 balls?

n-m-h3-dist-02.material: Box get 3 white balls and 2 black balls. Seoyun talk say, "Number X of white balls when dem draw 3 balls follow binomial distribution B(3, 3/5)." We no fit know from wetin dey written so far whether Seoyun correct.

n-m-h3-dist-02.s.s1.r.d: Order no matter for distribution of number X of white balls. Wetin decide whether na binomial distribution be whether the trials affect each other.

If dem put each ball back, that one hold; if dem no, earlier result change later probabilities. Dem don give number of balls, and number of trials no need to plenty.
n-m-h3-dist-02.s.s2.prompt: Suppose dem draw 3 balls without putting dem back. If first ball white, find probability say second one white, and use am explain why X no fit be B(3, 3/5) for this case.

n-m-h3-dist-02.s.s2.hint.1: Put that probability beside probability for first draw and compare dem.
